content: Oat sensitivity refers to an adverse reaction to the proteins found in oats, specifically Avena sativa. This sensitivity can arise due to an allergic response or a reaction to the seed storage proteins, which may occur either through ingestion or inhalation. In individuals with gluten-sensitive enteropathy (GSE), a more complex condition can develop, as they may also react to avenin, a protein in oats that is structurally similar to gluten found in wheat. Oat Allergy Research involving farmers exposed to grain dust and children with atopic dermatitis has demonstrated that oat proteins can act as allergens, affecting both the respiratory system and the skin. In studies of oat-dust sensitivity among farmers, 53% showed reactivity to oat dust, a rate second only to barley (70%) and nearly double that of wheat dust. A specific 66 kDa protein in oats was identified as reactive in 84% of tested sera, though some non-specific binding was observed, suggesting potential lectin-like interactions. Unlike the IgA and IgG antibody responses seen in celiac disease or dermatitis herpetiformis, such responses to avenins are not observed in atopic dermatitis patients. However, food allergies to oats can coexist with atopic dermatitis. Oat avenins share structural similarities with γand ω-gliadins of wheat, which may contribute to both enteropathic and anaphylactic responses. In cases of gluten-sensitive enteropathy, oat allergy can manifest in individuals who exhibit no histological abnormalities or T-cell reactions to avenin but may carry the rare DQ2.5 trans phenotype. Such individuals can experience anaphylactic reactions to avenin and conditions like wheat-dependent exercise-induced anaphylaxis. Avenin-Sensitive Enteropathy Gluten-sensitive enteropathy, including its severe form, celiac disease, is characterized by inflammation of the small intestinal tissue, leading to villus atrophy. The disease progresses from increased lymphocyte counts to villus flattening and crypt hyperplasia. Historically, oats were thought to cause celiac disease, but this misconception was largely due to contamination of oats with wheat, barley, or rye. Recent controlled studies on oat tolerance have identified avenin-sensitive enteropathy (ASE) in only 0.6% of the celiac population, based on a review of 165 cases. Immunological Evidence Anti-Avenin Antibodies In 1992, six oat proteins, including prolamins such as gamma avenin (CIP1), were identified as reactive with sera from celiac patients. Subsequent studies revealed that most celiac patients produce anti-avenin antibodies (AVA) with sensitivity and specificity comparable to anti-gliadin antibodies. However, these AVAs do not result from cross-reactivity with wheat proteins. Interestingly, AVA levels decline in celiac patients adhering to a gluten-free diet, even when oats are included, suggesting that oats alone do not sustain celiac disease in the absence of wheat. Cellular Immunity In gluten-sensitive enteropathy, prolamins interact with T-cells and antigen-presenting cells, while anti-transglutaminase antibodies mediate autoimmunity through covalent attachment to gliadin. In a study of 16 celiac patients, no significant Th1 immune response to avenins was observed, suggesting that avenins may not play a central role in celiac disease. However, a 2004 study identified exceptional cases of avenin-sensitive enteropathy. Among patients with symptoms triggered by a pure-oat challenge, three individuals exhibited elevated Marsh scores, avenin-responsive T-cells, and the DQ2.5/DQ2 phenotype. This phenotype, present in 25% of celiac patients, is associated with a higher risk of severe disease and gluten-sensitive enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma (GS-EATL). Synthetic avenin peptides, particularly in their deamidated form, elicited stronger immune responses, indicating that specific regions of avenin may dominate immune activation. Preliminary studies suggest that different oat strains may vary in their potential to trigger immunological responses in celiac patients, though further research is needed. Oats and Celiac Disease Recent studies indicate that most children and adults with celiac disease can tolerate oats, provided they are uncontaminated by other gluten-containing grains. Long-term studies (1, 2, and 5 years) have shown no significant changes in intestinal morphology or relapse of celiac disease in patients consuming oats. Levels of anti-gliadin and anti-reticulin antibodies, as well as intraepithelial lymphocyte (IEL) counts, did not differ significantly between oat-consuming and non-oat-consuming celiac patients in remission. In vitro tests sensitive to wheat gluten have demonstrated that avenin peptides do not induce endomysial antibody (EMA) production in cultured duodenal mucosa from celiac patients. Algorithms designed to predict T-cell stimulatory peptides in gluten identified many such peptides in hordeins and secalins but not in oat avenins. The Canadian Celiac Association recommends that adults can safely consume up to 70 grams of oats per day, while children can consume up to 25 grams. Some studies suggest that adults may tolerate up to 93 grams daily. There is no conclusive evidence that oats trigger gluten-sensitive enteropathy. However, in a small subset of celiac patients, oats may sustain or reinitiate disease once triggered by wheat. A recent study found that IEL counts were higher in oat-consuming celiac patients in remission, and anti-avenin antibody levels remained low on a gluten-free diet but increased when wheat was reintroduced. Estimates suggest that 0.5% to 20% of the celiac population may respond adversely to oats. Non-compliance with a gluten-free diet, including the consumption of oats in sensitive individuals, poses a risk for refractory disease and associated complications, including cancer.
